units.translation: where correctly, as it seems, Bambergerus [reads] ἑλκαίνουσι καὶ δεδηγμένοις [they fester and have been bitten], which the copyist changed to the singular number because of the preceding τῷ πρόσθεν [the one before].
Of things that prick the mind,
δακών [having bitten] Hirschig for δράκων [serpent], which see.
Biting the bit like a newly yoked colt.
Before such words one must bite one's tongue.
It would rot another by touching, though not bitten.
Crests and bells do not bite without the spear.
And this blood-dripping burden would be brought upon the house, with the former murder festering and having been bitten.
But most of all this misfortune bites.
I said this about her, that the people might be bitten.
they fester and have been bitten
Give him as food to the sea beasts.
Bearing the likeness of a most hateful beast, a monster.
The Argive monster destroyed the city.
What hateful monster could I call her and hit the mark?
Where someone is likely to bring tears upon the hearers.
They wet their bosoms with streaming tears.
The beds are filled with tears from longing for their husbands.

Since the poets do not seem to have said δάκρυ [tear] and δάκρυσι [with tears] except for metrical necessity, it follows that the genitive δακρύων [of tears] should be referred to δάκρυον [tear] rather than to δάκρυ [tear].
A mist full of tears rushed upon my eyes.
Joy creeps upon me, calling forth a tear.
Providing a life dimmed by tears.
A mournful shame drips from tears.
causing tears to fall, causing tears
causing tears to fall, causing tears
A stream dripping with tears from the eyes, flowing from the slender ones.
A lamentable hope of saving seed.

The old epic poets used this participle, both masculine and feminine δακρυχέουσα [shedding tears], not rarely, as with other similarly compounded participles: which the more recent poets did not notice, such as Nonnus, who said δακρυχέειν [to shed tears] and δακρυχέεσκε [he used to shed tears].
where Paleius seems rightly to delete οὔτε δακρύων [nor weeping].

How shall I weep for you?
It is possible to rejoice and weep at such things.

But no one, forbidding, keeps me from the halls of those pointed at with the finger (thus Schuetzius for δακτυλοδεικτῶν, which Casaubonus had changed to δακτυλόδεικτον).
i.e. with a throwing of the fingers. δακτυλόδικτον [thrown with the fingers] in Hesychius is a lemma without interpretation.
